tier_reason: The README tables show 2620ns (Protobuf) vs 132ns (ProtoCache), 8189 vs 270ns with reflection, and a twitter.proto serialize time of 215us (Protobuf) vs 101us (ProtoCacheEX). The benchmark code is public (test/benchmark/main.cc, protobuf.cc, protocache.cc, common.h), and CMakeLists.txt adds -march=native to the benchmark target. No compiler or CPU model is stated anywhere, so these are first-party numbers with partial methodology: C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Decode+traverse+dealloc 132ns vs Protobuf 2620ns (~19.8x); with reflection 270ns vs Protobuf 8189ns (~30.3x); ProtoCacheEX full serialization of twitter.proto 101us vs Protobuf 215us (~2.1x) (ratios derived from page data)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Compiler not stated. The CMake benchmark target (WITH_BENCHMARK=ON) adds -march=native (CMakeLists.txt), and the README build example uses CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release.
corrections.caveats: No CPU model or compiler is disclosed for the timing tables; the only flag known is -march=native from CMakeLists.txt. The comparison is not like-for-like: ProtoCache 'decode' is a zero-copy view cast over the buffer, while Protobuf does a full ParseFromString into an arena. FlatBuffers is faster on the same read test (89ns vs 132ns). ProtoCache loses elsewhere: serializing from a Protobuf message takes 6493ns vs 557ns for Protobuf (~11.7x slower), and its data is larger (780B vs 574B). The twitter.proto serialize functions (BenchmarkTwitterSerializePB/PC) exist in test/benchmark but main.cc does not call them, so that row cannot be reproduced from the harness as shipped. Small project (83 stars); numbers are first-party.

notes: All quoted numbers are on the README, and the Protobuf comparison is run in the same harness. I only added the '(derived from page data)' marker to the ratios and recorded the known flag. Metadata checks out via gh: BSD-3-Clause, 83 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2026-09-07 (active).

tier_reason: RESULTS.md (Native — Go table) shows goccy/go-json at 256.7 MB/s (8t) and 90.8 MB/s (1t), against encoding/json at 128.8 and 44.5 MB/s. The same harness runs both, unmarshalling into the same typed struct (golang/decoders.go, golang/bench.go, golang/parser.go). The Makefile gives a plain `go build` and go.mod requires Go 1.27.1, while RESULTS.md names the CPU (i7-6820HQ). Code, compiler, flags and CPU are all stated, so A.

corrections.workload: Unmarshal of 5 real SEC company-facts JSON files (39.9 MB total, 285,469 fact records) into the same typed Go structs, followed by the same fact-row reduction; goccy/go-json v0.10.5 vs encoding/json at 1/2/4/8 threads (GOMAXPROCS=threads, one file per work item), 20 timed passes after 2 warmups, in the third-party tegridy-benchie shootout
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go 1.27+ (go.mod: go 1.27.1); plain `go build` with GOFLAGS=-mod=mod GOPROXY=off and no extra flags (Makefile)
corrections.caveats: go-json's own README shows results only as chart images (from `go test -bench` in benchmarks/) with no CPU or Go version, so on its own it would be Tier C/D. The Tier-A number comes from tegridy-benchie instead, a third-party harness that is not well known: 0 stars, one commit, created 2026-09-23. It tested go-json v0.10.5 (Jan 2025), not v0.10.6 or current master, which rewrote parts of the decoder on 2026-09-24/25. go-json used more memory than encoding/json (peak RSS 409 vs 328 MB at 8t, 227 vs 158 MB at 1t). sonic was faster at 8 threads (260.0 MB/s). The corpus has only 5 files and work is split per file, so the 8-thread runs are limited to 5-way parallelism. The i7-6820HQ is 4 cores / 8 threads (the page says '8 cores').

notes: Numbers verified on RESULTS.md and results.json (go_goccy 256.74 / 90.83 MB/s; encoding/json 128.8 / 44.5). The ratios are correctly marked as derived. corrections.workload: Parsing 5 real SEC company-facts JSON files (39.9 MB total, 285,469 fact records) into a DOM (jiter 0.4.2 JsonValue vs serde_json 1.0.151 serde_json::Value) and reducing to fact rows with a shared reducer, at 1/2/4/8 threads (one file per work item), 20 timed passes after 2 warmups, in the third-party tegridy-benchie shootout
